still_true: Wegovy's US list price is still $1,349 a month on the branded box, and almost nobody pays it. The authorised generic and the ANDA generics sell beside it at a small fraction of that price.
The TrumpRx cash channel still operates, and oral Wegovy starting doses still cost $149 a month there. Oral semaglutide has no US generic.

The September 2027 tri-agency guidance allowing up to 30% premium differentials tied to verified adherence still stands, and Illinois's ban on adherence-conditioned premiums is still the only state ban in force.
The suicidal-ideation warning is still off every incretin label.

The FDA has approved no generic tirzepatide; Zepbound and Mounjaro are branded-only. Medicare still does not cover branded incretins for obesity alone, because the ~$41B CBO-scored branded benefit was never enacted.

population.note: FICTIONAL. Cycling arithmetic: 30.4% ever-used − 18.5% current = 11.9% of adults who used and are off now, about 2.1 points of them on a planned 'holiday'. About 60% of current users are on a second or later course (11.1 points), and 3.2 points cycled and are off again, so 14.3 / 30.4 ≈ 47% of ever-users have cycled. The other 8.7 points stopped once and have not restarted. This fits one-year persistence near one-third on weekly and oral products and 36–47% restarting within a year, with holidays now adding planned stops. Age check: 0.20×10.5 + 0.33×18 + 0.24×26.5 + 0.23×18 = 2.1 + 5.9 + 6.4 + 4.1 ≈ 18.5. Income thirds average 18.5. 18.5% of ~274M adults is ~50.7M users. FICTIONAL payer mix: Medicare 12.6M (24.9%), Medicaid 7.2M (14.2%) and the HRSA free-provision programme 2.2M (4.3%), so public payers cover 22.0M (43%), the largest single payer type, and ~60% of 2034 new starts. Commercial is 12.6M (25%), legitimate cash 9.4M (18.5%) and imported or counterfeit 6.5M (12.8%). Total 50.7M. Why the total fell despite cheaper drugs: about 2.1 points are on planned holidays at any moment; the Feb 2034 NAION warning drove stops among 50–64s with diabetes; the top third fell from 25 to 21 on holidays and 'off-drug lean' maintenance; calm plans shrank from 1.3M to ~0.8M; some brand users dropped out during forced switches to generics; and the 2034 counterfeit clusters produced abrupt stops. Gains came from Medicaid, HRSA and Medicare obesity-benefit starts, mostly in the bottom third: 12.0M of the bottom third's ~14.6M users are Medicaid 7.2M + HRSA 2.2M + ~2.6M gray market. Adult obesity is ~33.8%, edging up on regain. Roughly 21% of adults have obesity and have never used a drug, concentrated in the 21 states that have not opted into Medicaid coverage and among rural men. Pediatric: ~1.5% of under-18s are on a drug, ~3.0% of 12–17s and ~0.4% of 6–11s (liraglutide plus semaglutide after its Dec 2033 approval). New under-12 starts are now mostly Medicaid-paid. About 5.0M children live with a parent who has regained after stopping, and about 2.4M with a parent currently on a holiday.

access.public_coverage: Medicare reaches ~12.6M users. FICTIONAL arithmetic: ~6.4M are on branded products through the diabetes, CV, CKD, OSA and dementia-risk codes at ~$210 net × 12 ≈ $16.1B; ~6.2M are on generic semaglutide at ~$34 net × 12 ≈ $2.5B. Gross Part D incretin spend is therefore ~$18.6B, down from ~$31.6B in 2032, because diabetes users were switched to generic. Of the generic users, ~2.9M came in through the new obesity-only generic benefit created by the Generic Incretin Access Act (Jul 2033): 2.9M × $34 × 12 ≈ $1.2B a year. Medicaid: 29 states plus DC now cover generic semaglutide for obesity at a 90% federal match (Tennessee, Mississippi and Louisiana joined in 2034; Kentucky and New Mexico rejoined). Medicaid users total ~7.2M, of whom ~4.4M are on generic for obesity at ~$30 net: 4.4M × $30 × 12 ≈ $1.6B, ~$1.4B of it federal. The HRSA Community Metabolic Health Program ($1.0B a year) provides generic semaglutide free at ~1,300 FQHCs and IHS sites to uninsured adults at or below 200% FPL: ~2.2M × ~$28 (340B) × 12 ≈ $0.74B in drug cost plus nursing and administration. New federal spending is ~$1.2B + $1.4B + $1.0B ≈ $3.6B a year. The two state programmes that conditioned Medicaid coverage on adherence still do so.
access.generic_rest_of_world: Indian generic semaglutide sells for $3–25 a month and Chinese tirzepatide-analogue vials for $15–50. Chinese 'reta' (retatrutide-analogue) vials at $30–60 are now the fastest-growing gray product. Canadian and Brazilian generics have fallen to CAD 35–60 and BRL 120–220. India supplies most API for the US generics.
access.note: FICTIONAL. Generic injectable semaglutide (Viatris, Teva, Sandoz, Dr. Reddy's, Hikma, plus Novo's authorised generic) costs $39–69 a month cash at Cost Plus, Amazon and the chains, and $29 at the cheapest mail-order fills. Generic liraglutide is ~$29–45. Oral semaglutide has no generic: the Wegovy pill is $149 to start and $179 for maintenance on TrumpRx. Zepbound and Foundayo cut to $199–249. MariTide is $199 direct, with ~4.2M users. Retatrutide 12 mg lists at $1,299 and costs ~$449 cash direct, mostly on prior authorisation. Employer coverage rose from 30% to 41% because most new coverage is generic-only, with a $0–25 copay. Fewer commercial members use it (13.9M → 12.6M) because brand users were stepped to generics, holidays cluster in the top third and NAION stops followed the 2034 warning. Monitored metabolic tracks hold ~5.1M, ~3.6M of them on clinic MariTide. Weekly injectables are ~54% of users, orals ~37% and monthly ~9%. Gray market: ~6.5M users, down from 7.5M. It has shifted from semaglutide to Chinese 'reta' copies and to counterfeit 'US generic' pens sold by unlicensed online pharmacies. At least ~0.6M people counted as legitimate cash users received counterfeit product without knowing it.

on_market_classes: GLP-1 agonist, weekly injectable (semaglutide: Wegovy/Ozempic, plus US generics since Jan 2033)
GIP/GLP-1 dual agonist, weekly injectable (tirzepatide: Zepbound/Mounjaro)
GIP/GLP-1/glucagon triple agonist, weekly injectable (retatrutide, incl. 12 mg maintenance dose approved Nov 2033)
GLP-1 agonist/GIP-receptor antagonist antibody conjugate, monthly injectable (MariTide)
GLP-1 agonist, daily oral peptide (Wegovy pill 25 mg; Rybelsus; oral semaglutide for AUD and gambling disorder)
GLP-1 agonist, daily injectable (liraglutide: Saxenda, incl. generics)
Activin type II receptor antibody, lean-mass adjunct (bimagrumab, approved May 2034)
indications_beyond_weight_and_diabetes: pediatric obesity ages 6–11 (liraglutide incl. generics; injectable semaglutide approved Dec 2033), both with growth-velocity, Tanner and eating-disorder monitoring
reduction of risk of all-cause dementia in adults with obesity and established CVD (tirzepatide; confirmatory trial still ongoing)
alcohol use disorder, adjunct to psychosocial treatment (oral semaglutide, Mar 2033)
moderate-to-severe gambling disorder, adjunct to counselling (oral semaglutide, Apr 2034)
mainstream_offlabel_uses: compulsive shopping, screen and sexual-compulsion reduction, prescribed after the gambling label
'calm' and 'focus' microdosing, now ~0.8M subscribers and widely called sedating
generic injectable microdosing at home (0.1–0.25 mg) for 'steadiness'
dementia prevention by 50–70-year-olds without CVD, now mostly on $49 generic
planned 'drug holidays' used as a clinical protocol rather than a lapse
drugs.pipeline_note: FICTIONAL. Generic semaglutide entered the US in Jan 2033 on patent-settlement entry dates plus a Novo authorised generic; only the injectable is generic. Lilly filed retatrutide 12 mg as a higher maintenance dose of an existing product in Oct 2032. It was approved Nov 2033 at ~29% mean weight loss at 80 weeks, which realises the ~30% triple-agonist driver through a new dose rather than a new molecule. Semaglutide for ages 6–11 (STEP Young) was filed Nov 2032 and approved Dec 2033. The oral semaglutide AUD sNDA (filed Jan 2032) was approved Mar 2033. The gambling-disorder sNDA was filed Mar 2033 on a positive phase 3 and approved Apr 2034. Shopping, screen and sexual compulsion remain off-label. Bimagrumab (filed Jul 2032) was approved May 2034 as a lean-mass adjunct and has little uptake at $900+. The tirzepatide dementia confirmatory trial now reads out in 2035. Implants are still phase 1–2 and not on the market. No generic tirzepatide exists. US net incretin revenue fell ~15% from 2032 while US volume fell ~5%; global market ~$158B.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Still the leading cause of discontinuation. Retatrutide 12 mg titration produces higher early vomiting rates. Generic-switch periods caused a spike in GI complaints, mostly from titration being restarted wrongly.
Elevated with rapid weight loss and more frequent at the 29% loss level on retatrutide 12 mg.
No causal confirmation of acute pancreatitis; absolute risk low. Litigation centres on EPI.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled; EPI MDL in bellwether scheduling, and generic makers added as defendants in 2034.

safety_ledger.effect: Lean mass (muscle) loss and bone-density loss
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: FICTIONAL: Medicare hip-fracture HR ~1.3 after more than 2 years and ~1.45 after three or more cycles. Early retatrutide 12 mg data show greater lean-mass loss in absolute kg. Bimagrumab offers modest preservation.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Class warning retained; DXA code in use; resistance-training counselling on retatrutide, amycretin and generic semaglutide labels.

safety_ledger.effect: NAION (non-arteritic anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy) and optic-nerve injury
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: FICTIONAL: An FDA Sentinel analysis and a pooled Nordic registry (2033) found HR ~2.0–2.3 in semaglutide and tirzepatide users with type 2 diabetes, ~1.5 without diabetes. Absolute risk is ~2–4 per 10,000 person-years, rising with age and sleep apnoea, and the signal is similar across agonists. Most cases cause permanent partial vision loss in one eye.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Class Warnings and Precautions added Feb 2034 for all GLP-1-receptor agonists: stop promptly if sudden vision loss occurs, and consider baseline eye examination in diabetic users over 50. Medicare added an eye-exam code. EMA had listed it as very rare since 2025 and moved to a warning in 2034.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: No new signal in adults or adolescents.

safety_ledger.effect: Reward blunting / emotional flattening ('Ozempic personality', anhedonia)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: FICTIONAL: The FDA postmarketing observational study (Oct 2033) found clinically meaningful anhedonia at ~7% of users vs ~3% of matched controls, ~11% on retatrutide 12 mg and dose-related. Results at calm-plan doses were inconclusive but not null (~4.5%). Most users report milder 'evenness', and a majority of long-term users report taking at least one holiday to escape it.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Emotional blunting added to the postmarketing Adverse Reactions section in 2034, with no warning. The FDA warned that gambling-indication promotion may not imply effects on mood. Calm-plan untitled letters were not followed by enforcement.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: Half to two-thirds regain within 18 months. Planned holidays of 6–12 weeks show partial regain of ~2–4% of body weight, recovered on restart in most users. Holidays are not yet characterised for bone or pancreas.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: None directly; the AACE/Obesity Society 2034 statement gives holiday protocols as 'expert opinion'.

safety_ledger.prevalence_note: B12, iron and vitamin D deficiency. Deficiencies are more common among Medicaid and HRSA users with food insecurity. Low ferritin in adolescent girls persists.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Annual micronutrient panel language retained; HRSA programme funds the panel.

safety_ledger.effect: Exocrine pancreatic insufficiency after 5+ years of continuous use
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: FICTIONAL: ~2× EPI incidence after more than 5 years on semaglutide, and a small significant excess with tirzepatide now seen in a 2034 US claims analysis (~1.4×). Some partial recovery after 12+ months off.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Semaglutide EPI warning carried onto all generic labels; tirzepatide label update under negotiation.

safety_ledger.effect: Long-horizon effects beyond ~5 years; effects in adolescents and children on drug for decades; effects of repeated on/off cycling
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: About twelve years of semaglutide follow-up now exist. Holiday cycling is now deliberate and widespread, multiplying exposure to the poorly characterised on/off pattern.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Pediatric PMRs continue; FDA requested a cycling-and-bone study from Novo and Lilly in 2034.

safety_ledger.effect: Compounded / counterfeit / imported product harms (dosing errors, contamination, substitution)
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: FICTIONAL: In Jun 2034 CDC and FDA reported counterfeit 'generic semaglutide' pens that had entered three secondary wholesalers despite DSCSA tracing, plus Chinese 'reta' vials at 2–6× label. Together they caused ~2,100 ED visits for intractable vomiting, hypoglycaemia in insulin users and dehydration, and 14 deaths. Separately, confusion between generic vial concentrations (2.5 vs 5 mg/mL) and syringe units drove poison-centre calls to ~7× 2025 levels. Adverse-event reports tied to non-approved product passed ~41,000.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: FDA suspended two wholesaler licences, issued a DSCSA enforcement push and required standardised generic concentration labelling (Sep 2034). CBP seizures are ~3.5× 2030. Personal importation is still lightly enforced, with no new statute.

safety_ledger.effect: Growth deceleration, delayed puberty and restrictive eating in children started young
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: FICTIONAL: 36-month liraglutide PMR data show height-velocity deficit narrowing to ~0.5 cm/year, with partial catch-up in children who paused. The semaglutide 6–11 approval data (n≈600 over 68 weeks) were too short to assess growth. The Swedish ARFID HR held at ~1.8. Final adult height is still unknown.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Semaglutide 6–11 approved with 6-monthly growth velocity, Tanner staging and eating-disorder screening, plus a mandatory registry enrolment PMR. AAP keeps lifestyle-first guidance for prepubertal children. EMA restricted under-12 use to severe obesity with comorbidity.

safety_ledger.effect: Dysaesthesia, heart-rate increase and arrhythmia at high-dose triple agonism
safety_ledger.prevalence_note: FICTIONAL: Retatrutide 12 mg shows skin dysaesthesia in ~9% and resting heart-rate increases of 5–8 bpm. Atrial-fibrillation reports in users over 65 are under review.
safety_ledger.regulatory_response: Labelled in adverse reactions; cardiac postmarketing study required at approval.

food_and_beverage.state: About 34% of households have a current user, down slightly, but nearly half have a current or past user. Snack and confectionery volumes sit ~10% below 2025 and have been flat across the window as holidays and regain offset Medicaid starts. PepsiCo and Mondelez now sell 'holiday-week' portion packs. Kroger's zip-code planning has a new variable: stores near FQHC programme sites in Memphis and Jackson added protein bays for the first time. Pea protein has eased.

alcohol.state: Spirits volumes are ~14% below 2025 and beer ~9%. The AUD approval moved alcohol reduction from telehealth into primary care, and Medicaid in 29 states pays for it. Constellation and Molson Coors cut Midwest brewing capacity. NA and functional drinks gained shelf share but remain under 5% of volume.

restaurants.state: Traffic is flat. Portion-tiered menus are standard, and 'holiday menus' with larger plates appeared at Texas Roadhouse and regional steakhouses. QSR value menus hold in lower-income markets, although HRSA- and Medicaid-funded starts are slowly lowering regain-driven traffic in the Delta.

apparel.state: Plus-size specialists stabilised at a smaller base. Stretch, resale and 'two-size' wardrobes for holiday cyclers are the growth line. Tailoring for lifted bodies continues at the top.

fitness.state: Strength training keeps growing. Retatrutide 12 mg users are pushed into lean-mass programmes by label counselling. The HRSA programme funds a resistance-band and group-class add-on at some FQHCs. Premium DXA coaching is flat at $250–400 a month; budget lean-mass add-ons are $29.

insurance.state: Employer coverage rose to 41% on generic-only tiers, and pharmacy trend fell to ~+2% as semaglutide went generic. Part D premiums were flat in 2034 for the first time since 2028. Adherence differentials persist in self-insured firms with clinic MariTide tracks. Plans now require an eye-exam attestation for diabetic users over 50 on branded products.

pharma.state: Novo's US semaglutide revenue fell ~45% within a year of generic entry, and it cut ~3,000 US jobs in 2033, leaning on orals, CagriSema and amycretin. Lilly gained on retatrutide 12 mg and tirzepatide's protected patents. Amgen holds employer tracks. Viatris, Teva, Sandoz, Dr. Reddy's and Hikma split the generic volume. Counterfeit-defence and DSCSA spending rose again.

body_and_culture.what_the_body_signals: Being on it is unremarkable, and being off it is what needs explaining. The standard answer is 'I'm on a holiday'. Body shape still reads as payer, but the reading has coarsened: lean and lifted means commercial or cash brand; thin and soft means generic, public or plant clinic; very thin with a racing pulse in the gym means retatrutide 12 mg. Regained after 50 now prompts the question 'did your eyes make you stop?'
body_and_culture.thinness_and_class: Muscle remains the class uniform. In Charlotte and Austin, the elite move is the visible holiday: posting a summer off-drug and returning in September 'still lean'. In Memphis and the Mississippi Delta, TennCare and Mississippi Medicaid coverage plus FQHC free provision turned the cycler's face into the clinic's patient. The batch-history look is fading among the covered and persists among the 2.6M bottom-third gray users, many of them men buying 'reta' vials. Upper-income parents in Bethesda and Plano still avoid under-12 starts. In Medicaid families the semaglutide 6–11 approval is becoming routine paediatric practice.
body_and_culture.eating_as_ritual: Shared meals are shorter, except on 'holiday dinners', which are explicitly long. Bread Alone claims ~700 congregations and runs a paediatric-growth ministry. School debates now centre on whether nurses may store children's pens.
body_and_culture.dating_and_intimacy: Apps dropped 'calm plan' tags after the complaint went mainstream and now offer 'on holiday' and 'off' statuses. Couples time holidays together for anniversaries and conception attempts. Therapists report that the parallel-lives complaint is now described in standard terms: 'flat', 'dose it down', 'take August off'.
body_and_culture.meaning_of_appetite: Appetite is treated as a dosage setting. In the upper tier, its return on holiday is narrated as pleasure. In public-programme communities it is a clinic metric. Unmuted reframes its message around public provision, as 'the state is paying for flatness'. MAHA attacks the 6–11 semaglutide approval. Fat-acceptance revivalists remain separate from both.

interior_life.reward_blunting_prevalence_note: FICTIONAL: The FDA observational study found ~7% clinically meaningful anhedonia vs ~3% in controls, ~11% on retatrutide 12 mg and ~4.5% at calm-plan doses. Flatness is now a common complaint: national polling (Pew, 2034) finds ~48% of current users say the drug 'dulls' some pleasures. ~41% of users who have been on the drug for more than a year report at least one deliberate holiday or dose-down in the past year. About 2.1% of adults are on a holiday at any moment. Calm plans shrank to ~0.8M subscribers.
interior_life.framing: Side effect again, but a familiar and managed one, like a statin's aches. Clinicians and patients both talk of 'dose it down' and 'take a holiday'. Telehealth rebranded calm plans as 'adjustable'. The gambling and AUD labels reframe the same blunting as treatment when it is aimed at a compulsion.
interior_life.effect_on_work: ~5.1M employees remain in adherence-verified tracks. Holidays create a new conflict: track rules count a planned holiday as non-adherence, and Columbus-corridor workers lose premium differentials for taking one. The two EEOC charges were dismissed for lack of jurisdiction in 2033. Upper-tier firms put holiday weeks on shared calendars, alongside parental leave.
interior_life.effect_on_art_and_play: 'Holiday' became a genre: Netflix's 'August Off' and a run of essays on feeling food, music and lust return for six weeks. Sportsbook handle per active account fell again. DraftKings and FanDuel lobbied state gaming regulators against referring self-excluded bettors to the new indication, and New Jersey and Ohio did it anyway. Live music promoters report holiday-month ticket bumps.
interior_life.effect_on_intimacy: Desire mismatch is still the leading couples complaint. It is now usually solved by timing: synchronised holidays, a dose-down before vacations. Therapists see fewer 'calm to cope' partners and more disputes about who gets to take the holiday when there are children.
interior_life.effect_on_politics: Public provision made the drug a government programme, so the blunting complaint became a political one. Unmuted and some MAHA-aligned legislators call HRSA's programme 'subsidised sedation'. Democrats defend it as the end of the class gap. Republicans who voted for the Act cite the Part D savings. Still no turnout evidence of a 'sedated electorate'. Gaming states split over the gambling label.

state.regulatory_posture: Routine and permissive, with one more enforcement push than before. The FDA approved generics, retatrutide 12 mg, semaglutide 6–11, and the AUD and gambling labels. It imposed a NAION class warning, put postmarketing blunting language on labels, required standardised generic concentration labelling and suspended two wholesalers. No age restriction for children. Illinois remains the only state banning adherence premiums.
state.subsidy_or_mandate: The Generic Incretin Access Act (Jul 2033) lets Part D cover generic incretins for obesity, gives a 90% Medicaid match for generic weight-loss coverage and appropriates $1.0B a year to HRSA for free generic semaglutide at FQHCs and IHS sites, for a total of ~$3.6B a year in new federal spending (arithmetic in access.public_coverage). Branded incretins for obesity alone remain excluded. There is no mandate.
state.conditioning_or_surveillance: Two state Medicaid programmes still condition coverage on adherence and BMI progress. HRSA sites log fills and weights to a CDC surveillance registry, framed as counterfeit and NAION pharmacovigilance. Employer tracks still feed wellness vendors and now flag holidays. Telehealth mood check-ins still sell as de-identified cohorts.
state.workforce_or_military: TRICARE added generic semaglutide for obesity in 2034. The Army recruit pilot expanded to two more MEPS regions using generic. In Mar 2034 the DOT finally issued guidance allowing commercial drivers to use incretins for AUD with a medical-examiner review and banning calm-plan microdosing during duty.
state.geopolitics_of_supply: US generics depend on Indian API, which gave New Delhi leverage in stalled trade talks. US–India talks now pair API inspection access with mail enforcement, and still no agreement. Chinese 'reta' copies dominate gray growth. Beijing again rejected FDA import-alert naming. The US cash-to-Indian-generic gap has fallen from ~40–50× to ~3–10×.

events.event: FDA approves the first generic semaglutide injectables as patent-settlement entry dates arrive, and Novo launches an authorised generic the same week; by July, cash prices are $39–69 a month at Cost Plus, Amazon and the major chains

Congress passes the Generic Incretin Access Act in a health extenders package: Part D may cover generic incretins for obesity, Medicaid gets a 90% match for generic weight-loss coverage, and HRSA receives $1.0B a year to give generic semaglutide free at community health centres

FDA approves retatrutide 12 mg (filed Oct 2032) at ~29% average weight loss, and in December approves semaglutide for children aged 6–11 (filed Nov 2032) with mandatory growth-velocity monitoring and registry enrolment

FDA adds a class warning for sudden optic-nerve vision loss (NAION) to every GLP-1 drug label after Sentinel and Nordic registry data show roughly double the risk in diabetic users; Medicare creates an eye-exam code and ophthalmology referrals spike
FDA approves oral semaglutide for moderate-to-severe gambling disorder (filed Mar 2033), a year after its alcohol-use-disorder approval; New Jersey and Ohio begin referring self-excluded bettors

CDC and FDA tie counterfeit 'generic semaglutide' pens found in three secondary wholesalers, and super-concentrated Chinese 'reta' vials, to ~2,100 ER visits and 14 deaths; two wholesalers are suspended and standard concentration labelling is ordered

open_tensions: Public money now buys the drug that a widely shared complaint says dulls pleasure, and HRSA's registry and two adherence-conditioned Medicaid programmes mean the poorest users are the most measured. 'Subsidised sedation' is a campaign line heading into 2036.

Holidays are mainstream practice and unstudied. Millions of people deliberately cycle a drug whose cycling effects on bone, pancreas and now optic nerve are uncharacterised, while employer tracks penalise the same holidays as non-adherence.
Children aged 6–11 can now be started on semaglutide, Medicaid pays for it, and the monitoring the label requires falls on the clinics least able to provide it. No one yet knows final adult height.

Generics closed the price gap, but counterfeits moved into the gap's new shape: fake 'US generic' pens inside licensed supply chains and Chinese 'reta' copies of the 29% drug, which is still $449 legitimately. 6.5M people still buy outside the system, and the NAION warning now applies to products no one is tracking.

prose.headline: Fifty Dollars, Free at the Clinic, and 'I'm on a Holiday': The Year the Shot Went Public
prose.world_in_600_words:
At the end of 2034 slightly fewer Americans take an incretin drug than two years ago, about 18.5 percent of adults, roughly fifty-one million people, even though the drug has never been cheaper. Semaglutide went generic in January 2033. By summer a month's pen cost less than fifty dollars at the chains and less than thirty by mail. Six months later Congress did what it had refused to do at branded prices. It let Medicare pay for the generic for obesity, gave states a ninety percent match to cover it in Medicaid, and funded community health centres to hand it out free to the uninsured poor. Public programmes are now the largest payer. Most people starting the drug in 2034 start it on the government.

The number fell anyway, and the reasons are ordinary. The first is the holiday. The complaint that the drugs flatten pleasure stopped being a niche worry and became something everyone says. An FDA study counted one heavy user in nine on the new high-dose retatrutide losing a real share of pleasure, and nearly half of all users say the drug dulls something. Doctors answer with dose-downs and planned breaks, six weeks off in August or a month before a wedding. At any moment about two adults in a hundred are on a holiday. Being on the drug is unremarkable. Being off it needs an explanation, and the explanation is usually that one.

The second reason is the eye. In February the FDA put a class warning on every GLP-1 label for sudden optic-nerve vision loss, a risk measured in a few cases per ten thousand people each year but roughly doubled in diabetics. Some fifty-five-year-olds stopped. Others now carry an eye-exam form.

The third is the counterfeit. Cheap generics did not end the mail trade; they changed its shape. Chinese copies of retatrutide, the triple agonist whose new twelve-milligram dose takes off nearly thirty percent of body weight and still costs $449 legitimately, are now the fastest-growing gray product. In June federal agencies traced fake 'generic' pens that had got inside three wholesalers, along with overstrength vials, to about two thousand emergency visits and fourteen deaths. Poison-centre calls run seven times what they were a decade ago, many from people confusing one generic vial strength with another.

The labels widened in two directions. In December 2033 semaglutide was approved for children six to eleven, with growth measured every six months, because the earlier liraglutide data still showed slower height gain and no one knows final adult height. In April oral semaglutide was approved for gambling disorder, a year after alcohol. Some sportsbooks lobbied gaming regulators against sending self-excluded bettors to their doctors, and New Jersey and Ohio sent them anyway. So the dulling that users complain of is also, for some patients, the treatment.

The map shifted. In Memphis and the Mississippi Delta, where the cycler's face used to show the batch history, Tennessee and Mississippi joined the Medicaid option and the clinic van replaced the WhatsApp reseller for many women. The gray market there is now mostly men buying 'reta'. In Charlotte the status move is a visible August off and a lean return. On the Columbus freight corridor the plant clinic still gives the monthly shot, and a holiday costs you your premium discount.

Part D spending fell by a third when diabetics were switched to generic. That saving is the reason the law passed and the reason it is hard to attack. Critics now call it subsidised sedation. The country looks steadier than it did, and some of that steadiness is a public programme.
prose.a_day_in_the_life:
Denise Coleman picks up her pen at the Christ Community clinic on Third Street at 7:40, before her first client. Free. The nurse weighs her, types, and slides a yellow sheet across: eye exam, you're over fifty, you're diabetic, it's on the label now. Denise folds it into her scrub pocket with the bus card.

Mr. Albright, 81, wants his eggs scrambled soft. She makes three and eats none, which he notices. "You on that government shot?" She says she is. He says his daughter's on a holiday, eating like a teenager, happy as a clam. Denise says she's heard holidays are nice.

At lunch her sister Tanya texts a photo of a vial with Chinese characters and RETA in marker. Forty dollars. Tanya's on the Medicaid list since spring but says the generic is slow and she wants the thirty percent. Denise types don't, deletes it, types the news said people died, deletes that, sends a heart.

The afternoon client is new, a boy of nine whose mother asks Denise to measure him against the doorframe because the clinic needs it every six months and she works doubles. Denise marks the pencil line. Last line was June. They both look at the gap and neither says how small it is.

On the bus home she watches a man across the aisle laugh at his phone for a long time. She tries to remember the last thing that made her laugh like that. She can't decide whether that's the drug or the job.

She calls the eye doctor. First opening, March.
